summary: Describes two reference video traffic models for evaluating RTP congestion control: a statistical model of a live encoder responding to rate requests, and a trace-driven one based on real encoded frame sizes. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Fake video sources that behave like real cameras, so people can test whether their network sharing rules work fairly.

questions: video traffic model for congestion control
subtitle: Reference models for synthetic video traffic to test RTP congestion control.

tldr.problem: When testing congestion control algorithms for real-time video, synthetic traffic sources need to behave like real video encoders, including handling rate changes sluggishly and producing output that fluctuates around the target rate.
tldr.mechanism: This document describes two reference models: a statistical model that characterizes encoder behavior through parameters like reaction latency and output fluctuation, and a trace-driven model that uses real encoder output traces recorded from actual video sequences.
tldr.outcome: Tests using these models can evaluate RTP congestion control more realistically than simple synthetic sources, allowing fair comparison across different algorithm candidates before deployment.

today: RFC 8593 provides the standard video traffic models used in RTP congestion control research and evaluation. The reference implementation (Syncodecs) remains available for researchers testing new algorithms.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Evaluating RTP congestion control algorithms requires traffic that mimics real-world video encoder behavior. Unlike synthetic traffic sources that conform perfectly to rate requests, a live video encoder responds sluggishly to rate changes and deviates from the target rate due to encoder rate-control uncertainties. This document presents two approaches for modeling this behavior, allowing algorithm evaluation to focus on the congestion control itself rather than codec-specific quirks.
sections.plainLanguage: When you test whether a traffic control system works, you need to use fake video that acts like real video encoders—not instantly changing and with some wobbliness in the output.

sections.title: Desired Behaviors
sections.content:
A synthetic video source should support five key capabilities: changing bitrate by adjusting frame rate or resolution; fluctuating around the target bitrate; showing delay in convergence to target rate; generating intra-coded (I) frames on demand; and varying frame-rate and resolution dynamically.

The model should also balance several characteristics: low computational complexity; temporal pattern similarity to real encoders; statistical resemblance in mean, variance, peak, and autocorrelation; and wide coverage of different codec and content behaviors. The document emphasizes that temporal patterns must vary across different time scales from tens of milliseconds to sub-seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Fake video should act like real video: it changes bitrate slowly, it wobbles around the target rate, it can be a bit jumpy, and different types of video have different characteristics.

sections.title: Statistical Reference Model
sections.content:
The statistical model characterizes encoder behavior through tunable parameters. Encoder reaction latency (tau_v) represents the delay before responding to rate changes—typically 0.2 seconds. During this transient period, output frames show high variation: a burst frame (K_B) much larger than average may be followed by smaller frames.

At steady state, the model uses Laplacian distributions to characterize fluctuations in both frame interval and frame size around reference values. SCALE_t controls frame interval variance, and SCALE_b controls frame size variance. The output is clipped within a dynamic range [R_min, R_max] dictated by video content complexity.

The model uses simple parameters that can be fitted from empirical data captured from real encoders, making it flexible for different codecs and content types.
sections.plainLanguage: The statistical model says: the encoder takes about 0.2 seconds to react to a rate change, during which it might send a huge frame followed by smaller ones. Then it settles to wobbling around the target using a mathematical formula for the wobble. You can tune this formula for different types of video.

sections.title: Trace-Driven Model
sections.content:
The trace-driven model uses real encoder output traces: frame sizes recorded from actual video encoding at various target bitrates. The process involves three steps: encode a representative video sequence (2 to 4 minutes long) at multiple bitrates using a real encoder; store the frame-size sequences in a lookup map; and upon a rate request, interpolate between the closest stored bitrate sequences.

When the target rate falls between stored bitrates, linear interpolation produces realistic frame sizes. When the target rate exceeds available traces, the model scales upward from the highest stored rate. The model maintains state (r_current for bitrate, t_current for frame index) to track position in the trace and cycle through frames.

This approach naturally exhibits temporal fluctuations and patterns matching real encoder output, but requires collecting and storing trace data for each codec and content type of interest.
sections.plainLanguage: The trace-driven model says: run a real video camera and encoder to record what frame sizes it produces at different bitrates, then look up those stored frame sizes when you need to fake the video. If you need a bitrate in between, just blend between two recordings.

sections.title: Combining the Two Approaches
sections.content:
A hybrid model uses the trace-driven approach for steady-state behavior (when the rate is stable or changing slightly) and the statistical model for transient behavior (when rate changes are substantial, such as exceeding 10% of previous rate). During transient periods, the model generates K_d frames using statistical parameters, then reverts to trace-driven output at steady state.

This combination leverages the strengths of both approaches: realistic temporal patterns from traces and flexible, parameter-driven handling of rate transitions. The transient period also respects the encoder's time-damped response defined by tau_v.
sections.plainLanguage: The best way is to use recorded frame sizes when things are steady, but switch to the statistical model when the bitrate changes a lot. That way you get real behavior in both cases.

sections.title: Reference Implementation
sections.content:
The document notes that statistical, trace-driven, and hybrid models have been implemented as a stand-alone, platform-independent module available as open-source software (Syncodecs). This implementation can be integrated into network simulators such as ns-2 and ns-3, as well as real network testbeds.

Researchers can use these implementations to evaluate congestion control algorithms with synthetic video traffic that realistically models encoder behavior, improving the reliability of algorithm comparison before deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone wrote code that does all this. You can use it in simulators or with real networks to test your congestion control ideas with realistic fake video.

left.title: Statistical model
left.desc: Flexible, tunable, good for transients. Requires parameter fitting.

right.title: Trace-driven model
right.desc: Realistic, temporal patterns match real output. Requires trace collection.
